# II. EXTENDED KALMAN FILTER FOR DYNAMIC STATE ESTIMATION

Since the basic Kalman filter is limited to a linear assignment, it is generally extended when there is nonlinearity associated with either the process model or the measurement model or both. The extended Kalman filter (EKF) is the nonlinear version of Kalman filter which linearizes about an estimate of the current mean and error covariance.

The main steps of the extended Kalman filter are summarized as follows [11].

1) The discrete time system equations of a non-linear system can be presented as \[x_{k+1} = f_k(x_k, u_k, w_k)\] \[y_k = h_k(x_k, v_k)\] \[w_k \sim (0, Q_k)\] \[v_k \sim (0, R_k)\]  
2) The initial state of EKF is initialized by taking the expectation of the initial state of the system and the initial state covariance matrix is initialized by taking the second moment of the system state about initial estimate. Mathematically, it can be expressed as follows.  

\[\begin{array}{rl} & {\hat{x}_0^+ = E(x_0)}\\ & {P_0^+ = E[(x_0 - \hat{x}_0^+)(x_0 - \hat{x}_0^+)^T]} \end{array} \quad (2)\]  

3) For each time step \(k\) , the prediction of state and error covariance matrix is done as follows.  

a) Partial derivative matrices of the current state estimate \(\hat{x}_k^+ \) are computed as follows.  

\[F_{k} = \left. \begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial f_{k}}{\partial x}\\ \frac{\partial x_{k}}{\partial x} \end{array} \right|_{\hat{x}_k^+} \quad (3)\]  

\[L_{k}=\frac{\partial f_{k}}{\partial w}\Big|_{\hat{x}_{k-1}^{+}} \quad (4)\]  

b) The time update of state estimate and estimation-error covariance matrix is performed using:  

\[\begin{array}{r}P_{k}^{-} = F_{k}P^{+}k - 1F_{k}^{T} + L_{k}Q_{k}L_{k}\\ \hat{x}_{k}^{-} = f_{k}(\hat{x}_{k^{-}1}^{+},u_{k - 1},0) \end{array} \quad (5)\]  

4) For each time step \(k\) , the correction of state and error covariance matrix is done as follows.  

a) Partial derivative matrices for correction are computed as:  

\[H_{k} = \left. \begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial h_{k}}{\partial x} \\ \hat{x}_{k}^{-} \\ V_{k} = \left. \begin{array}{c}\frac{\partial h_{k}}{\partial x} \\ \hat{x}_{k}^{-} \\ V_{k} = \left. \begin{array}{c}H_{k} \\ \frac{\partial h_{k}}{\partial v} \\ \hat{x}_{k}^{-} \\\ \hat{v}_{k} \end{array} \right|}_{\hat{x}_{k}^{-}} \end{array} \right. \quad (5)\]  

b) The measurement update of the state estimate and estimation error covariance is performed as follows:  

\[\begin{array}{c}{K_{k} = P_{k}^{-}H_{k}^{T}(H_{k}P_{k}^{-}H_{k}^{T} + V_{k}R_{k}V_{k}^{T})^{-1}}\\ {\hat{x}_{k}^{+} = \hat{x}_{k}^{-} + K_{k}[z_{k} - h_{k}(\hat{x}_{k}^{-},0)]}\\ {P_{k}^{+} = (I - K_{k}H_{k})P_{k}^{-}} \end{array} \quad (6)\]  

III. UNSENTED KALMAN FILTER FOR DYNAMIC STATE ESTIMATION

When the process model and measurement model are highly nonlinear, the EKF may give poor performance [12]. This is because of the propagation of the error covariance through linearization of the underlying nonlinear model. In such cases, the unscented Kalman filter (UKF) can be used, which uses a deterministic sampling technique known as the unscented transformation (UT) to generate a minimum set of sample points (referred to as sigma points) around the mean [12]. These sigma points are then transformed through the nonlinear functions, from which the estimates of new mean and error- covariance are computed. In some of the applications, UKF is applied to reduce the computational cost of the estimation, as there is no requirement to calculate Jacobians.

The main steps of the unscented kalman filter are summarized as follows [11].

1) Let us consider we have the n-state discrete-time system as in (1). 2) We initialize UKF similar to that of EKF using (2). 3) To time update the states from one measurement time to another following steps are performed. a) Choose sigma points to propagate from \(k - 1\) to \(k\) time step using recent best guess of \(P\) and \(\hat{x}\) as follows. \[\hat{x}_{k-1}^{+} = \hat{x}_{k-1}^{+} + \hat{x}^{(i)} \quad i = 1, \dots , 2n\] \[\hat{x}^{(i)} = \left( \sqrt{n P_{-\mathrm{k}}^{-1} + \Gamma} \right)^{\mathrm{T}} \quad i = 1, \dots , n\] \[i^{(i+n)} = -\left( \sqrt{n P_{k-1}^{+} + \Gamma} \right)^{\mathrm{T}} \quad i = 1, \dots , n  \] b) Using appropriate changes on the nonlinear function \(f(.)\) to transform the sigma points into \(\hat{x}_{k}^{(i)}\) .  

\[x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}x_{(i)}(i) \quad (2)\]  

b) Using appropriate changes on the nonlinear function \(f(.)\) to transform the sigma points into \(\hat{x}_k^{(i)}\) .  

\[\hat{x}_k^{(i)} = f(x_{k - 1}^{(i)},u_k,t_k) \quad (8)\]  

c) Obtain the priori state estimate by combining \(\hat{x}_k^{(i) \text{vector as follows.}\)  

\[\hat{x}_k^- = \frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i = 1}^{2n}\hat{x}_k^{(i)} \quad (9)\]

## 3 Methodology

We first determine the rotor angle $\alpha $ from the measured derivative of speed and angular velocity for each trial separately:

\[\dot{\alpha} = \frac{\text{d}}{ \text{d}t} (v \text{cos}(R ) + \omega \text{sin} (R ))  = 0 \]

\[\alpha = \text{atan} \frac{ \text{d}(v \text{cos}(R ) + \omega \text{sin} (R ) )}{ \text{d}t} \]

We first determine the rotor angle $\alpha$ from the measured derivative of speed and angular velocity for each trial separately:

\[\dot{\alpha} = \frac{\text{d}}{ \text{d}t} (v \text{cos}(R ) + \omega \text{sin} (R ))  = 0\]

\[\alpha = \text{atan} \frac{ \text{d}(v \text{cos}(R ) + \omega \text{sin} (R ) )}{ \text{d}t}\]

When the angular velocity and the rotor angle stay within $[-10, 10]^{\circ}$, $[-\pi, \pi)$ acceptance angle limit and KF noise limit, the rotor angle is guaranteed to be correct, so the rotor will move with EKF algorithm. Furthermore, to prevent the rotation overruns, the rotor angles and angular velocity values, which can deviate from the nominal speed, need to be modified accordingly. Below is an example, where the truck travels in clockwise direction.

\[\begin{aligned} R &= 13, ||v_t|| &= 30 \frac{\text{m/s}}{\omega} \\ \alpha &= 0.3 \alpha,\ \omega &= 10 \frac{\text{rad/s}}{\omega}\end{aligned}\] \[T = \frac{1}{\omega}\Delta R\] \[\begin{aligned} v'1 &= 13 \frac{\text{m/s}}{\omega} && \Delta v_1 = v1 \end{aligned}\] \[\begin{aligned} v'2 &= 0 \Delta v_2 = v2 - v'2 \\ t1 &= 50 \Delta t_1 && \Delta t_1 = t2 - t1, ||t_1|| =0.1 \end{aligned}\]

The system state equation using EKF algorithm can be written as:

\[\Delta \bar{x} = A \Delta x_A + B \Delta u\]

With the output

\[\Delta v = \Delta f + \Delta g\]

where

\[\Delta x = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta \bar{x_{\theta}} \\ \Delta \bar{x_{\phi}} \end{bmatrix}, \ \Delta u = A \Delta \bar{x}, \ \Delta v = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta f_1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \Delta f_2 \end{bmatrix}, \ \Delta f = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \ \Delta f_1 = 1, \ \Delta f_2 = 0, \ \Delta g = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \ \Delta g_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\] \[A = \begin{pmatrix} -0.215 \\ 0.003 \\ 0.043 \\ 0.003 \\ 2.414 \\ 23.75 \end{pmatrix} \quad B = \begin{bmatrix} 70 \\ -0.45 \\ 0 \\ 70 \\ 70 \\ 1.25 \end{bmatrix}\]

Since only two speed values are available, the first iteration of the EKF algorithm will be:

\[v1 = \frac{\Delta f1}{\Delta t_1} + v1^u\] \[v2 = \Delta f2 - v'2 \Delta t_1 + v'2\]

where

\[v_1v_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ - \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, v_1' = 13, \ v_2' = -\Delta f_2\]

## 3 Experimental Results and Analysis

### Overall Consideration

The optimization results shown in section 2 and 3 utilize untrusted trajectory data delivery from UKF to stochastic acceleration sensor for components 1 and 3. However, due to the use of stochastic technique, the difference in coordinate and terminal pose values between UKF estimated motion and real motion is negligible. Considering the approximation error of the different ranging discretization scheme used in different components, the error in the actual distance \(d\) between the mobile robot and the vehicle is small [11]. Therefore, the spacing error \(e_{x}\), \(e_{y}\) of kinematic controlling system between the mobile robot and Kinamba (the vehicle where we running) is negligible when each component is not stabilized.

## 4 Conclusion

In this paper, we adopted the state estimator for kinematic control system which allows rigid links to continuously rotate about their axes but not the wheel axis. In addition, one simple approach used for kinematic controlling system is the proposed KaMPA system, it consists of five independent tracking control loop stiffened motors which has maximum one degree of freedom at their ends. It is used to achieve precise kinematic controlling by eliminating the demand for numerous precise axis angles. It can be explained with the following equations for 5 axes kinematic controlling system connected to Oxford Kinamba with 6MP 400-W Mitsubishi Electric DC25WD3164E. For the four wheeled mobile robot system with 26Kg Rover, model 4014, the sum speed closed loop ratio of \(\delta\)=5.3887 is small enough, so the tracking controller can apply a good control effect.
